terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to fit pages to the pager, find the hill someone meant, and cut a message down to one line.

tasks.title: Lines that fit the pager
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `pager.py`, write the line that imports the `textwrap` module, with `import`. Then write a function called `pager_lines` that takes a message, as text, and a width, a whole number, and gives back a list of the lines of the message, none wider than the width, made by the module's `wrap`. For `page` and `24` the first line is `'Callout to Scarth Fell,'`. Print what it gives back for `page` and `24`.

Check calls `pager_lines` with messages and widths of its own, one with a word longer than the width, and looks at what it gives back and whether it was made by `textwrap`'s `wrap`.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on import and on reading a module's page.
Write the import line, then the def line of pager_lines.
Reach wrap through the module's name, give it the message and the width, and give back what it gives you.
Print what pager_lines gives back for page and 24, and run the file.
hints: After `import textwrap`, everything in the module is reached through its name and a dot.
`wrap` takes the text and the width, and already gives back a list of lines. Nothing else needs doing to it.
The shape is `return textwrap.wrap(message, width)` inside `pager_lines`, with `import textwrap` above the function.

videos.title: What a module is, and importing one

tasks.title: The closest hill
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, find the function on the page of the `difflib` module that gives back the closest matches to a word from a list of words, and import that function by itself with `from`. Then write a function called `closest_hill` that takes a hill as someone typed it, as text, and a list of hills, and gives back the closest hill on the list, or `None` when no hill is close enough. Use the function's usual cutoff for close enough. For `"Scarth Fel"` and `hills` it gives back `'Scarth Fell'`. Print what it gives back for `"Scarth Fel"` and `hills`.

Check calls `closest_hill` with hills of its own, some typed wrong, one close to none, and looks at what it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on reading a module's page.
Open the difflib page from Read up, and look through its list of functions for one about close matches.
Import it by itself with from, and print what it gives back for "Scarth Fel" and hills.
Give back the closest hill from what it gives you, or None when it gives you nothing.
hints: The functions of a module are listed near the top of its page, each with a sentence on what it does. Look for one whose name and sentence speak of close matches.
It takes the word and the list of possibilities, and gives back a list, the closest first. An empty list means nothing was close enough. Its `n` says how many to give back at most.

The shape is `from difflib import get_close_matches` above the function, then `matches = get_close_matches(typed, hills, n=1)` inside it, and `matches[0]` when `matches` is not empty, `None` otherwise.

tasks.title: A one-line summary
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a function called `summary` that takes a message, as text, and a width, and gives back the message cut down to fit that width by `textwrap`'s `shorten`. The file already has a function called `shorten`, Ailsa's, and her radio desk still calls it: import `textwrap`'s `shorten` so that hers keeps its name and keeps working. For `page` and `40` it gives back `'Callout to Scarth Fell, north-east [...]'`. Print what `summary` gives back for `page` and `40`, then print `shorten("ECHO ONE")`.

Check calls `summary` with messages and widths of its own, then calls `shorten` with call signs of its own, after the lines under `# Task 3` have run.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on as and on why import * is a trap.
Write an import that gives textwrap's shorten a name the file does not use yet.
Run the file and look at what shorten("ECHO ONE") prints: it should still be the short call sign.
hints: An import with `from` makes a name in your file, and a name can stand for only one thing. If it is a name the file already uses, the new thing takes its place.
`as` after an import gives what is imported a name of your choosing. Importing the whole module works too: its functions are then reached through the module's name.
The shape is `from textwrap import shorten as cut_to` above the function, and `return cut_to(message, width)` inside `summary`.
